claim: NMDARs act as coincidence detectors in Hebbian plasticity by fluxing Ca2+ when simultaneously depolarized and glutamate bound in the textbook view.
source: In the textbook view, NMDA receptors (NMDARs) act as coincidence detectors in Hebbian plasticity by fluxing Ca2+ when simultaneously depolarized and glutamate bound.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, representing the traditional understanding of NMDAR function.

claim: Hebbian coincidence detection requires that NMDARs be located postsynaptically.
source: Hebbian coincidence detection requires that NMDARs be located postsynaptically, but enigmatic presynaptic NMDARs (preNMDARs) also exist.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the requirements for Hebbian coincidence detection.

claim: Presynaptic NMDARs exist.
source: Hebbian coincidence detection requires that NMDARs be located postsynaptically, but enigmatic presynaptic NMDARs (preNMDARs) also exist.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract.

claim: PreNMDARs regulate neurotransmitter release.
source: It is known that preNMDARs regulate neurotransmitter release, but precisely how remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: NMDARs can signal non-ionotropically, without the need for Ca2+ flux.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that NMDARs can also signal non-ionotropically, without the need for Ca2+ flux.
evidence: This is stated as emerging evidence from the literature.

claim: At synapses between developing visual cortex layer-5 pyramidal cells, preNMDARs rely on Mg2+ and RIM1αβ to regulate evoked release during periods of high-frequency firing.
source: At synapses between developing visual cortex layer-5 (L5) pyramidal cells (PCs), preNMDARs rely on Mg2+ and Rab3-interacting molecule 1αβ (RIM1αβ) to regulate evoked release during periods of high-frequency firing, but they signal non-ionotropically via c-Jun N-terminal kinase 2 (JNK2) to regulate spontaneous release regardless of frequency.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: PreNMDARs signal non-ionotropically via JNK2 to regulate spontaneous release regardless of frequency at L5 PC→PC synapses.
source: At synapses between developing visual cortex layer-5 (L5) pyramidal cells (PCs), preNMDARs rely on Mg2+ and Rab3-interacting molecule 1αβ (RIM1αβ) to regulate evoked release during periods of high-frequency firing, but they signal non-ionotropically via c-Jun N-terminal kinase 2 (JNK2) to regulate spontaneous release regardless of frequency.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Timing-dependent long-term depression (tLTD) at L5 PC→PC synapses depends on preNMDARs but not on frequency.
source: At the same synapses, timing-dependent long-term depression (tLTD) depends on preNMDARs but not on frequency.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: tLTD at L5 PC→PC synapses was abolished by presynaptic but not postsynaptic NMDAR deletion.
source: We found that tLTD at L5 PC→PC synapses was abolished by pre- but not postsynaptic NMDAR deletion, cementing the view that tLTD requires preNMDARs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 using sparse knockout of GluN1 subunit.

claim: tLTD prevailed after channel pore blockade with MK-801.
source: In agreement with non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling, tLTD prevailed after channel pore blockade with MK-801, unlike tLTP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3 using MK-801.

claim: tLTP was abolished by channel pore blockade with MK-801.
source: In agreement with non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling, tLTD prevailed after channel pore blockade with MK-801, unlike tLTP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 using MK-801.

claim: Homozygous RIM1αβ deletion did not affect tLTD.
source: Homozygous RIM1αβ deletion did not affect tLTD, but wash-in of the JNK2 blocker SP600125 abolished tLTD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 using Emx1Cre/+; RIM1αβfl/fl mice.

claim: Wash-in of the JNK2 blocker SP600125 abolished tLTD.
source: Homozygous RIM1αβ deletion did not affect tLTD, but wash-in of the JNK2 blocker SP600125 abolished tLTD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 using SP600125.

claim: A peptide blocking the interaction between JNK2 and Syntaxin-1a abolished tLTD if loaded presynaptically but not postsynaptically, regardless of frequency.
source: Consistent with a presynaptic need for JNK2, a peptide blocking the interaction between JNK2 and Syntaxin-1a (STX1a) abolished tLTD if loaded pre- but not postsynaptically, regardless of frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 using JGRi1 peptide.

claim: Low-frequency tLTD was not blocked by the channel pore blocker MK-801.
source: Finally, low-frequency tLTD was not blocked by the channel pore blocker MK-801, nor by 7-CK, a non-competitive NMDAR antagonist at the co-agonist site.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 using MK-801 at low frequency.

claim: Low-frequency tLTD was not blocked by 7-CK, a non-competitive NMDAR antagonist at the co-agonist site.
source: Finally, low-frequency tLTD was not blocked by the channel pore blocker MK-801, nor by 7-CK, a non-competitive NMDAR antagonist at the co-agonist site.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 using 7-CK.

claim: Neocortical L5 PC→PC tLTD relies on non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling via JNK2/STX1a.
source: We conclude that neocortical L5 PC→PC tLTD relies on non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling via JNK2/STX1a.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Synaptic plasticity is thought to underlie information storage.
source: Such synaptic plasticity is thought to underlie information storage (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Malenka and Bear, 2004; Nabavi et al., 2014) as well as developmental circuit refinement (Cline, 1998; Katz and Shatz, 1996; Song and Abbott, 2001), an idea often attributed to Hebb, 1949.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Synaptic plasticity is thought to underlie developmental circuit refinement.
source: Such synaptic plasticity is thought to underlie information storage (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Malenka and Bear, 2004; Nabavi et al., 2014) as well as developmental circuit refinement (Cline, 1998; Katz and Shatz, 1996; Song and Abbott, 2001), an idea often attributed to Hebb, 1949.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the STDP paradigm, coincident firing in the range of tens of milliseconds results in long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy.
source: In the STDP paradigm, coincident firing in the range of tens of milliseconds results in long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy (Feldman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In classic STDP studies, presynaptic spikes leading postsynaptic spikes by a few milliseconds drive timing-dependent long-term potentiation (tLTP).
source: In classic STDP studies (Bi and Poo, 1998; Feldman, 2000; Markram et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 1998), presynaptic spikes leading postsynaptic spikes by a few milliseconds drive timing-dependent long-term potentiation (tLTP), whereas the opposite temporal ordering elicits timing-dependent tLTD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In classic STDP studies, postsynaptic spikes leading presynaptic spikes elicit timing-dependent tLTD.
source: In classic STDP studies (Bi and Poo, 1998; Feldman, 2000; Markram et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 1998), presynaptic spikes leading postsynaptic spikes by a few milliseconds drive timing-dependent long-term potentiation (tLTP), whereas the opposite temporal ordering elicits timing-dependent tLTD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: STDP rules and mechanisms depend on factors such as synapse type, developmental stage, and neuromodulation.
source: However, STDP is quite diverse, with rules and mechanisms depending on factors such as synapse type, developmental stage, and neuromodulation (Debanne and Inglebert, 2023; Larsen and Sjöström, 2015; McFarlan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Many forms of STDP critically depend on NMDARs.
source: Many forms of STDP critically depend on NMDARs, which are a subfamily of glutamatergic receptors known for forming heterotetrameric ligand-gated ion channels (Paoletti et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMDARs are a subfamily of glutamatergic receptors known for forming heterotetrameric ligand-gated ion channels.
source: Many forms of STDP critically depend on NMDARs, which are a subfamily of glutamatergic receptors known for forming heterotetrameric ligand-gated ion channels (Paoletti et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Action potentials initiated at the soma are thought to backpropagate through dendrites.
source: Action potentials initiated at the soma are thought to backpropagate through dendrites (Stuart and Sakmann, 1994) to elicit nonlinear calcium signals localized to dendritic spines (Koester and Sakmann, 1998) by activating glutamate-bound NMDARs in the postsynapse (Yuste and Denk, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Backpropagating action potentials elicit nonlinear calcium signals localized to dendritic spines.
source: Action potentials initiated at the soma are thought to backpropagate through dendrites (Stuart and Sakmann, 1994) to elicit nonlinear calcium signals localized to dendritic spines (Koester and Sakmann, 1998) by activating glutamate-bound NMDARs in the postsynapse (Yuste and Denk, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Backpropagating action potentials elicit calcium signals by activating glutamate-bound NMDARs in the postsynapse.
source: Action potentials initiated at the soma are thought to backpropagate through dendrites (Stuart and Sakmann, 1994) to elicit nonlinear calcium signals localized to dendritic spines (Koester and Sakmann, 1998) by activating glutamate-bound NMDARs in the postsynapse (Yuste and Denk, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMDARs are able to act as classic detectors of coincident EPSPs and action potentials in postsynaptic neurons because of their dual need for presynaptically released glutamate as well as postsynaptic depolarization to relieve the Mg2+ blockade and flux the Ca2+ that triggers tLTP.
source: These NMDARs are thus able to act as classic detectors of coincident EPSPs and action potentials in postsynaptic neurons (Markram et al., 1997) because of their dual need for presynaptically released glutamate as well as postsynaptic depolarization to relieve the Mg2+ blockade and flux the Ca2+ that triggers tLTP (Sjöström and Nelson, 2002; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At L5 PC→PC connections, tLTD relies on preNMDAR signaling.
source: We previously found evidence that, at L5 PC→PC connections, tLTD relies on preNMDAR signaling (Sjöström et al., 2003; Sjöström et al., 2007), but precisely how was not clear (Duguid and Sjöström, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: The presynaptic spike is long gone by the time preNMDARs bind the released glutamate.
source: After all, the presynaptic spike is long gone by the time preNMDARs bind the released glutamate, arguing that another presynaptic spike must arrive soon enough to depolarize and unblock glutamate-bound preNMDARs, suggesting a need for high-frequency spiking (Duguid and Sjöström, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about the timing of presynaptic events.

claim: Another presynaptic spike must arrive soon enough to depolarize and unblock glutamate-bound preNMDARs, suggesting a need for high-frequency spiking.
source: After all, the presynaptic spike is long gone by the time preNMDARs bind the released glutamate, arguing that another presynaptic spike must arrive soon enough to depolarize and unblock glutamate-bound preNMDARs, suggesting a need for high-frequency spiking (Duguid and Sjöström, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as an inference supported by citation.

claim: tLTD is readily induced at low frequencies.
source: Yet tLTD is readily induced at low frequencies (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: PreNMDARs differentially regulate evoked and spontaneous release via RIM1aß and JNK2, respectively.
source: More recently, we found that preNMDARs differentially regulate evoked and spontaneous release via RIM1aß and JNK2, respectively (Abrahamsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: The JNK-mediated regulation of spontaneous release by preNMDARs was not Mg2+-sensitive.
source: Interestingly, the JNK-mediated regulation of spontaneous release by preNMDARs was not Mg2+-sensitive (Abrahamsson et al., 2017), revealing the existence of an unconventional form of non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling in the axon (Bouvier et al., 2018; Dore et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: An unconventional form of non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling exists in the axon.
source: Interestingly, the JNK-mediated regulation of spontaneous release by preNMDARs was not Mg2+-sensitive (Abrahamsson et al., 2017), revealing the existence of an unconventional form of non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling in the axon (Bouvier et al., 2018; Dore et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from prior findings, supported by citations.

claim: If tLTD relied on non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling, it would explain why it can be induced at both low and high frequencies.
source: If tLTD relied on such non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling, it would explain why it can be induced at both low and high frequencies, since in this signaling mode, preNMDARs are sensitive to glutamate but not to Mg2+ or membrane potential.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about the implications of non-ionotropic signaling.

claim: In non-ionotropic signaling mode, preNMDARs are sensitive to glutamate but not to Mg2+ or membrane potential.
source: If tLTD relied on such non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling, it would explain why it can be induced at both low and high frequencies, since in this signaling mode, preNMDARs are sensitive to glutamate but not to Mg2+ or membrane potential.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about non-ionotropic signaling.

claim: L5 PC→PC tLTD relies on the non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling pathway mediated by JNK2.
source: We found that, regardless of frequency, L5 PC→PC tLTD relies on the non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling pathway mediated by JNK2, which helps to resolve the long-standing enigma surrounding its lack of frequency dependence (Duguid and Sjöström, 2006).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: High-frequency tLTD at 20 Hz was intact in WT→KO connections where postsynaptic NMDARs were deleted.
source: In this wild-type (WT) → KO sample, HF tLTD at 20 Hz (see Methods) was intact (after/before = 68%, p<0.001), suggesting postNMDARs were not required.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: High-frequency tLTD at 20 Hz was abolished in KO→WT connections where presynaptic NMDARs were deleted.
source: For this KO→WT sample, however, the same induction elicited no plasticity (after/before = 100%, p=0.99), suggesting tLTD needed preNMDARs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HF tLTD was robustly evoked for presynaptic WT but not presynaptic KO pairs.
source: HF tLTD was robustly evoked for presynaptic WT (Pre WT, blue) but not presynaptic KO pairs (Pre KO, red), verifying the need for preNMDARs in tLTD that we previously demonstrated (Sjöström et al., 2003; Sjöström et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: CV analysis indicated that tLTD was presynaptically expressed.
source: CV analysis indicated that tLTD was presynaptically expressed (φ=19°±4°, n=8, one-sample t-test vs. diagonal, p0.001), in agreement with our prior studies (Sjöström et al., 2003; Sjöström et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by CV analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MK-801 abolished tLTP at L5 PC→PC synapses.
source: MK-801 is known to block hippocampal LTP (Nabavi et al., 2013) as well as tLTP at excitatory inputs onto neocortical L2/3 PCs (Bender et al., 2006; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Rodríguez-Moreno et al., 2011). At L5 PC→PC synapses, tLTP relies on different NMDARs than tLTD (Sjöström et al., 2003), but the MK-801 sensitivity has, to our knowledge, not been explored. Here, we found that MK-801 wash-in abolished potentiation (Figure 2), suggesting that L5 PC→PC tLTP relies on ionotropically signaling postNMDARs, like tLTP at other neocortical synapses (Bender et al., 2006; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: L5 PC→PC tLTP relies on ionotropically signaling postNMDARs.
source: Here, we found that MK-801 wash-in abolished potentiation (Figure 2), suggesting that L5 PC→PC tLTP relies on ionotropically signaling postNMDARs, like tLTP at other neocortical synapses (Bender et al., 2006; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the MK-801 blockade of tLTP shown in Figure 2.

claim: MK-801 wash-in had no effect on baseline responses elicited at low frequency.
source: We also verified that MK-801 wash-in had no effect on baseline responses elicited at low frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as expected (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Buchanan et al., 2012; Sjöström et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MK-801 had no effect on tLTD at L5 PC→PC synapses.
source: However, MK-801 had no effect on tLTD (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HF tLTD and LF tLTD were not differentially affected by MK-801.
source: Since the action of MK-801 is activity and voltage-dependent (Huettner and Bean, 1988), we were concerned that HF tLTD and low-frequency (LF) tLTD (see Methods) might be differentially affected by this drug, but we found no difference (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: tLTD at both low and high frequencies in MK-801 was robust compared to no-induction MK-801 controls.
source: Ensembles revealed robust tLTD at both low and high frequencies in MK-801 (blue triangles) compared to no-induction MK-801 controls (gray, Welch ANOVA p<0.01), suggesting that tLTD does not rely on ionotropic NMDAR signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: tLTD does not rely on ionotropic NMDAR signaling.
source: Ensembles revealed robust tLTD at both low and high frequencies in MK-801 (blue triangles) compared to no-induction MK-801 controls (gray, Welch ANOVA p<0.01), suggesting that tLTD does not rely on ionotropic NMDAR signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of tLTD in MK-801 shown in Figure 3.

claim: CV analysis indicated that tLTD at both HF and LF induction frequencies was presynaptically expressed.
source: CV analysis indicated that tLTD at both induction frequencies was presynaptically expressed (HF LTD: φ=13°±5°, n=6, p<0.05; LF LTD: 15°±4°, n=5, p<0.05), in agreement with our prior findings (Figure 1; Sjöström et al., 2003; Sjöström et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by CV analysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 7-CK suppressed synaptic responses.
source: In control experiments, we found that 7-CK suppressed synaptic responses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) in a manner consistent with its known additional action as a competitive inhibitor of L-glutamate transport into synaptic vesicles (Bartlett et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 7-CK was unable to block tLTD.
source: With this approach, we found that 7-CK was unable to block tLTD (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: tLTP but not tLTD requires ionotropic NMDAR signaling.
source: A parsimonious interpretation of these experiments is that tLTP but not tLTD requires ionotropic NMDAR signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of MK-801 on tLTP and tLTD.

claim: The interpretation that tLTP but not tLTD requires ionotropic NMDAR signaling helps to explain why tLTD is not frequency dependent.
source: This interpretation additionally helps to explain why tLTD is not frequency dependent (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Ionotropic preNMDAR-mediated regulation of evoked release at L5 PC→PC synapses relies on RIM1αβ.
source: We previously found that ionotropic preNMDAR-mediated regulation of evoked release at L5 PC→PC synapses relies on RIM1αβ (Abrahamsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: RIM1α is required for endocannabinoid-mediated LTD in hippocampus.
source: Additionally, RIM1α is required for endocannabinoid-mediated LTD in hippocampus (Castillo et al., 2002; Chevaleyre et al., 2007) as well as for LTP in amygdala (Fourcaudot et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RIM1α is required for LTP in amygdala.
source: Additionally, RIM1α is required for endocannabinoid-mediated LTD in hippocampus (Castillo et al., 2002; Chevaleyre et al., 2007) as well as for LTP in amygdala (Fourcaudot et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: L5 PC→PC tLTD was robust in Emx1Cre/+; RIM1αβfl/fl animals.
source: We found that L5 PC→PC tLTD was robust in Emx1Cre/+; RIM1αβfl/fl animals (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The magnitude of tLTD in Emx1Cre/+; RIM1αβfl/fl mice was indistinguishable to that in WT mice.
source: The magnitude of tLTD in Emx1Cre/+; RIM1αβfl/fl mice was furthermore indistinguishable to that in WT mice (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: PPR and CV analysis both suggested a presynaptic site of expression for tLTD in RIM1αβ deletion mice.
source: To explore the locus of expression of tLTD, we analyzed paired-pulse ratio (PPR) and CV, which both suggested a presynaptic site of expression (Figure 5E and F), like we found before (Figures 1, 3E and 4D; Sjöström et al., 2003; Sjöström et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by PPR and CV analysis data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Homozygous RIM1αβ deletion had no detectable effect on L5 PC→PC tLTD.
source: Homozygous RIM1αβ deletion thus had no detectable effect on L5 PC→PC tLTD.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The JNK2-blocker SP600125 abolished tLTD.
source: For this sample connection, the JNK2-blocker SP600125 (Bennett et al., 2001) abolished tLTD (after/before = 99%, p=0.86).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: tLTD after homozygous RIM1αβ deletion was indistinguishable from WT tLTD.
source: Ensemble data revealed that tLTD after homozygous RIM1αβ deletion (blue) was indistinguishable from WT tLTD (black), thereby dissociating tLTD from RIM1αβ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: SP600125 robustly disrupted tLTD, with an outcome indistinguishable from no-induction controls.
source: However, SP600125 robustly disrupted tLTD (red), with an outcome indistinguishable from no-induction controls (gray). Welch ANOVA p<0.001.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: tLTD increased PPR compared to controls, suggesting presynaptic expression.
source: tLTD increased PPR (black and blue) compared to controls (gray), suggesting presynaptic expression. Welch ANOVA p<0.05.
evidence: This is supported by PPR analysis data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CV analysis indicated that tLTD was presynaptically expressed, whether RIM1αβ was deleted or not.
source: CV analysis indicated that tLTD was presynaptically expressed, whether RIM1αβ was deleted (φ=16°±4°, n=10, p<0.01) or not (φ=13°±2°, n=15, p<0.001), in agreement with our prior findings (Figures 1 and 3E, Figure 4D; Sjöström et al., 2003; Sjöström et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by CV analysis data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: tLTD relies on JNK2 but not on RIM1αβ.
source: Taken together, our results show that tLTD relies on JNK2 but not on RIM1αβ.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: When JGRi1 peptide was loaded presynaptically, HF tLTD was abolished.
source: When loaded presynaptically, HF tLTD was abolished, whereas when loaded postsynaptically, HF tLTD could be induced (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: When JGRi1 peptide was loaded postsynaptically, HF tLTD could be induced.
source: When loaded presynaptically, HF tLTD was abolished, whereas when loaded postsynaptically, HF tLTD could be induced (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: tLTD was expressed presynaptically in JGRi1 peptide experiments.
source: As before, tLTD was expressed presynaptically (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by PPR and CV analysis data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: tLTD was mediated by preNMDAR signaling via the JNK2/STX1a complex.
source: This suggested that tLTD was mediated by preNMDAR signaling via the JNK2/STX1a complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the JGRi1 peptide experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The JGRi1 peptide ought to block tLTD at any frequency.
source: By comparison with preNMDAR regulation of spontaneous release via JNK2 — which was independent of Mg2+ and frequency (Abrahamsson et al., 2017) — this also suggested that the JGRi1 peptide ought to block tLTD at any frequency.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from prior findings.

claim: When JGRi1 peptide was loaded presynaptically, LF tLTD was abolished.
source: As for HF tLTD, when the peptide was loaded presynaptically, LF tLTD was abolished, whereas when loaded postsynaptically, LF tLTD was expressed by presynaptic downregulation of release (Figure 6G–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-L.

claim: When JGRi1 peptide was loaded postsynaptically, LF tLTD was expressed by presynaptic downregulation of release.
source: As for HF tLTD, when the peptide was loaded presynaptically, LF tLTD was abolished, whereas when loaded postsynaptically, LF tLTD was expressed by presynaptic downregulation of release (Figure 6G–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-L.

claim: At low frequency, preNMDARs remained blocked by Mg2+.
source: We note that at low frequency, preNMDARs remained blocked by Mg2+ (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2024), so this outcome lends further support to the view that tLTD requires non-ionotropic signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: The outcome that LF tLTD persists when preNMDARs are blocked by Mg2+ lends further support to the view that tLTD requires non-ionotropic signaling.
source: We note that at low frequency, preNMDARs remained blocked by Mg2+ (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2024), so this outcome lends further support to the view that tLTD requires non-ionotropic signaling.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The sensitivity to pre- but not postsynaptic peptide cements the view that non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling is located presynaptically.
source: The sensitivity to pre- but not postsynaptic peptide further cements the view that this form of NMDAR signaling is located presynaptically.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Regardless of induction frequency, tLTD is mediated by non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling via the JNK2/STX1a complex in presynaptic neurons.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that, regardless of induction frequency, tLTD is mediated by non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling via the JNK2/STX1a complex in presynaptic neurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The study provides resolution to the long-standing enigma about the role of preNMDARs in tLTD by showing for the first time that tLTD relies on non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling via JNK2.
source: The role of preNMDARs in tLTD has long been enigmatic (Duguid and Sjöström, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2003). Our study provides resolution to this long-standing enigma by showing for the first time that tLTD relies on non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling via JNK2.
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings challenge the traditional view of NMDA receptors as ionotropic coincidence detectors.
source: Our findings thereby further challenge the traditional view of NMDA receptors as ionotropic coincidence detectors and reveal how non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling can shape STDP.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the study's findings.

claim: Non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling can shape STDP.
source: Our findings thereby further challenge the traditional view of NMDA receptors as ionotropic coincidence detectors and reveal how non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling can shape STDP.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the study's findings.

claim: Evidence for preNMDARs has been reported for decades.
source: Although evidence for preNMDARs has been reported for decades (Aoki et al., 1994; Berretta and Jones, 1996; DeBiasi et al., 1996; Glitsch and Marty, 1999; Liu et al., 1997), this receptor type has been controversial.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDARs have been controversial.
source: Although evidence for preNMDARs has been reported for decades (Aoki et al., 1994; Berretta and Jones, 1996; DeBiasi et al., 1996; Glitsch and Marty, 1999; Liu et al., 1997), this receptor type has been controversial.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the history of preNMDAR research.

claim: One study could not find the preNMDARs that underlie L5 PC→PC tLTD.
source: For instance, one study (Christie and Jahr, 2009) could not find the preNMDARs that we reported as underlying L5 PC→PC tLTD (Sjöström et al., 2003; Sjöström et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Several studies largely corroborated the findings of preNMDARs at L4 PC → L2/3 PC synapses and elsewhere.
source: Several other studies, however, largely corroborated our findings of preNMDARs at L4 PC → L2/3 PC synapses and elsewhere (Banerjee et al., 2014; Banerjee et al., 2009; Bender et al., 2006; Brasier and Feldman, 2008; Corlew et al., 2007; Rodríguez-Moreno and Paulsen, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One study argued that the NMDARs that underlie L4 PC → L2/3 PC tLTD are actually postsynaptic.
source: Then again, one study argued that the NMDARs that underlie L4 PC → L2/3 PC tLTD are actually postsynaptic (Carter and Jahr, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Similar disagreements about preNMDARs exist in cerebellum, with some studies reporting preNMDARs and others arguing that they do not exist.
source: Similar disagreements exist in cerebellum, with some studies reporting preNMDARs (Casado et al., 2000; Casado et al., 2002; Glitsch and Marty, 1999) and others arguing that they do not exist (Christie and Jahr, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDARs often require high-frequency spike trains to activate.
source: Consistently, preNMDARs often require high-frequency spike trains to activate (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Bidoret et al., 2009; Buchanan et al., 2012; McGuinness et al., 2010; Sjöström et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2021), as a single spike that elicits glutamate release is gone by the time preNMDARs bind the glutamate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDARs govern spontaneous release.
source: However, preNMDARs also govern spontaneous release (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Berretta and Jones, 1996; Buchanan et al., 2012; Kunz et al., 2013; Sjöström et al., 2003) and tLTD (Sjöström et al., 2003), which both occur at low frequencies, leading to a long-standing contradiction in the field (Banerjee et al., 2009; Duguid and Sjöström, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDARs governing spontaneous release and tLTD at low frequencies has led to a long-standing contradiction in the field.
source: However, preNMDARs also govern spontaneous release (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Berretta and Jones, 1996; Buchanan et al., 2012; Kunz et al., 2013; Sjöström et al., 2003) and tLTD (Sjöström et al., 2003), which both occur at low frequencies, leading to a long-standing contradiction in the field (Banerjee et al., 2009; Duguid and Sjöström, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the controversy in the field.

claim: PostNMDARs are ubiquitously expressed.
source: Whereas postNMDARs are ubiquitously expressed, preNMDARs are only found at specific synapse types (Banerjee et al., 2014; Brasier and Feldman, 2008; Buchanan et al., 2012; Larsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: PreNMDARs are only found at specific synapse types.
source: Whereas postNMDARs are ubiquitously expressed, preNMDARs are only found at specific synapse types (Banerjee et al., 2014; Brasier and Feldman, 2008; Buchanan et al., 2012; Larsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDARs are easy to miss if different synapse types are mixed experimentally.
source: PreNMDARs are thus easy to miss if different synapse types are mixed experimentally.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the synapse-specific nature of preNMDARs.

claim: PreNMDARs often rely on particular subunits and conditions that reduce the flux of Ca2+.
source: Furthermore, preNMDARs often rely on particular subunits and conditions that reduce the flux of Ca2+ (Banerjee et al., 2009; Kunz et al., 2013; Larsen et al., 2011), leading to weak signals that may be hard to detect.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDARs can signal non-ionotropically to control release.
source: Finally, preNMDARs can also signal non-ionotropically to control release (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling has been reported in classic LTD.
source: However, non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling has been reported broadly, for instance, in classic LTD (Nabavi et al., 2013; Nielsen et al., 2024; Park et al., 2022), structural plasticity (Park et al., 2022; Stein et al., 2021; Thomazeau et al., 2021), and ischemic excitotoxicity (Weilinger et al., 2016), so this mode of NMDAR signaling is not necessarily rare.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling has been reported in structural plasticity.
source: However, non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling has been reported broadly, for instance, in classic LTD (Nabavi et al., 2013; Nielsen et al., 2024; Park et al., 2022), structural plasticity (Park et al., 2022; Stein et al., 2021; Thomazeau et al., 2021), and ischemic excitotoxicity (Weilinger et al., 2016), so this mode of NMDAR signaling is not necessarily rare.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling has been reported in ischemic excitotoxicity.
source: However, non-ionotropic NMDAR signaling has been reported broadly, for instance, in classic LTD (Nabavi et al., 2013; Nielsen et al., 2024; Park et al., 2022), structural plasticity (Park et al., 2022; Stein et al., 2021; Thomazeau et al., 2021), and ischemic excitotoxicity (Weilinger et al., 2016), so this mode of NMDAR signaling is not necessarily rare.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-ionotropic signaling has been found for kainate receptors.
source: In fact, non-ionotropic signaling has also been found for other ionotropic channels, such as kainate receptors (Rodríguez-Moreno and Lerma, 1998), AMPA receptors (Takago et al., 2005; Wang and Durkin, 1995), and even voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Trus and Atlas, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Non-ionotropic signaling has been found for AMPA receptors.
source: In fact, non-ionotropic signaling has also been found for other ionotropic channels, such as kainate receptors (Rodríguez-Moreno and Lerma, 1998), AMPA receptors (Takago et al., 2005; Wang and Durkin, 1995), and even voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Trus and Atlas, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-ionotropic signaling has been found for voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: In fact, non-ionotropic signaling has also been found for other ionotropic channels, such as kainate receptors (Rodríguez-Moreno and Lerma, 1998), AMPA receptors (Takago et al., 2005; Wang and Durkin, 1995), and even voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Trus and Atlas, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The classic textbook view of receptor types as strictly ionotropic or non-ionotropic is not solidly anchored in the biology.
source: The classic textbook view of receptor types as strictly ionotropic or non-ionotropic is, therefore, not solidly anchored in the biology.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the evidence of non-ionotropic signaling in various receptor types.

claim: The finding that preNMDAR signaling in L5 PC→PC tLTD is non-ionotropic explains why this form of plasticity does not depend on frequency.
source: Our finding that preNMDAR signaling in L5 PC→PC tLTD is non-ionotropic explains why this form of plasticity does not depend on frequency (Duguid and Sjöström, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the study's findings.

claim: In non-ionotropic signaling mode, there is no need for spikes to arrive in quick succession to provide the depolarization that would be required for ionotropic preNMDAR signaling.
source: This is because, in this signaling mode, preNMDARs are sensitive to glutamate but not to Mg2+ or membrane potential, so there is no need for spikes to arrive in quick succession to provide the depolarization that would be required for ionotropic preNMDAR signaling (Duguid and Sjöström, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the properties of non-ionotropic signaling.

claim: The finding that non-ionotropically signaling preNMDARs are key to L5 PC→PC tLTD aligns with much of the prior literature while simultaneously bringing closure to long-standing controversies.
source: Overall, our finding that non-ionotropically signaling preNMDARs are key to L5 PC→PC tLTD thus aligns with much of the prior literature while simultaneously bringing closure to long-standing controversies (Bouvier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the study's findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: The genetic deletion approach firmly situates the NMDARs needed for tLTD in the pre- rather than the postsynaptic cell of L5 PC→PC pairs.
source: Our genetic deletion approach furthermore firmly situates the NMDARs needed for tLTD in the pre- rather than the postsynaptic cell of L5 PC→PC pairs (Carter and Jahr, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic deletion experiments.

claim: JNKs are serine-threonine kinases that belong to the mitogen-activated protein kinase family and mediate stress stimuli.
source: JNKs are serine-threonine kinases that belong to the mitogen-activated protein kinase family and mediate stress stimuli, e.g., cytokines, ultraviolet irradiation, and heat shock.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about JNKs.

claim: There are three closely related vertebrate JNK genes: JNK1 and JNK2 are ubiquitous, while JNK3 is primarily neuronal.
source: There are three closely related vertebrate genes: JNK1 and JNK2 are ubiquitous, while JNK3 is primarily neuronal (Yamasaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the brain, JNKs are key developmental regulators, for instance, of neuronal migration, dendrite formation, and axon maintenance.
source: In the brain, JNKs are key developmental regulators, for instance, of neuronal migration, dendrite formation, and axon maintenance (Yamasaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: tLTD at L5 PC→PC connections requires simultaneous activation of preNMDARs and endocannabinoid CB1 receptors.
source: We previously demonstrated that tLTD at L5 PC→PC connections requires simultaneous activation of preNMDARs and endocannabinoid CB1 receptors (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: JNK is activated by NMDARs.
source: It has long been known that JNK is activated by NMDARs (Coffey, 2014; Mukherjee et al., 1999) as well as by CB1 receptors (Rueda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: JNK is activated by CB1 receptors.
source: It has long been known that JNK is activated by NMDARs (Coffey, 2014; Mukherjee et al., 1999) as well as by CB1 receptors (Rueda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDARs regulate spontaneous release by signaling via JNK2.
source: More recently, we and others established that preNMDARs regulate spontaneous release by signaling via JNK2 (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Nisticò et al., 2015) and that this regulation critically depends on an interaction between JNK2 and STX1a (Marcelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDAR regulation of spontaneous release critically depends on an interaction between JNK2 and STX1a.
source: More recently, we and others established that preNMDARs regulate spontaneous release by signaling via JNK2 (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Nisticò et al., 2015) and that this regulation critically depends on an interaction between JNK2 and STX1a (Marcelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It was previously proposed that JNK2 signaling is involved in behavioral learning.
source: Interestingly, it was previously proposed that JNK2 signaling is involved in behavioral learning as well as in classical NMDAR-dependent LTD (Curran et al., 2003; Morel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It was previously proposed that JNK2 signaling is involved in classical NMDAR-dependent LTD.
source: Interestingly, it was previously proposed that JNK2 signaling is involved in behavioral learning as well as in classical NMDAR-dependent LTD (Curran et al., 2003; Morel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: This study is the first to show a need for JNK2 signaling specifically in tLTD.
source: Our study, however, is to our knowledge the first to show a need for JNK2 signaling specifically in tLTD, which relies on mechanistic underpinnings that differ from classical LTD, such as retrograde endocannabinoid signaling (Bender et al., 2006; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: tLTD relies on mechanistic underpinnings that differ from classical LTD, such as retrograde endocannabinoid signaling.
source: Our study, however, is to our knowledge the first to show a need for JNK2 signaling specifically in tLTD, which relies on mechanistic underpinnings that differ from classical LTD, such as retrograde endocannabinoid signaling (Bender et al., 2006; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The activation of JNK2 is achieved by non-ionotropic preNMDAR action.
source: Furthermore, in our hands, the activation of JNK2 is achieved by non-ionotropic preNMDAR action.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The present study extends the prior literature by suggesting that JNK2 signaling may be a general principle that applies to distinct forms of long-term plasticity.
source: Our present study thus extends the prior literature by suggesting that JNK2 signaling may be a general principle that applies to distinct forms of long-term plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the study's findings.

claim: Several studies of tLTD at L4 PC → L2/3 PC synapses reported that MK-801 abolishes tLTD.
source: In our hands, the NMDAR channel pore blocker MK-801 surprisingly did not block tLTD at L5 PC→PC connections, even though several other studies of tLTD at L4 PC → L2/3 PC synapses reported that MK-801 abolishes tLTD (Banerjee et al., 2014; Larsen et al., 2014; Rodríguez-Moreno et al., 2013; Rodríguez-Moreno et al., 2011; Rodríguez-Moreno and Paulsen, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The difference in MK-801 sensitivity is likely due to non-ionotropic versus ionotropic preNMDAR tLTD at L5 PC→PC and L4 PC → L2/3 PC synapses, respectively.
source: This difference is likely due to non-ionotropic versus ionotropic preNMDAR tLTD at L5 PC→PC and L4 PC → L2/3 PC synapses, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the study's findings.

claim: The mechanistic distinction between non-ionotropic and ionotropic preNMDAR tLTD is generally consistent with the view that STDP depends on synapse type.
source: This mechanistic distinction is generally consistent with the view that STDP depends on synapse type (Larsen and Sjöström, 2015; McFarlan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated as an inference supported by citations.

claim: tLTD is mediated by distinct mechanisms even for different synaptic input types onto the same L2/3 PCs.
source: In fact, tLTD is mediated by distinct mechanisms even for different synaptic input types onto the same L2/3 PCs (Banerjee et al., 2009; Larsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At L4 PC → L2/3 PC synapses, a frequency-dependent form of presynaptic self-depression has been reported.
source: Indeed, at L4 PC → L2/3 PC synapses, a frequency-dependent form of presynaptic self-depression has been reported (Rodríguez-Moreno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Frequency dependence of tLTD does not exist at L5 PC→PC connections.
source: Such frequency dependence of tLTD does not, however, exist at L5 PC→PC connections (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDARs at L5 PC→PC connections signal ionotropically to boost neurotransmitter release during high-frequency firing.
source: Curiously, preNMDARs at L5 PC→PC connections signal ionotropically to boost neurotransmitter release during high-frequency firing (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Buchanan et al., 2012; Sjöström et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ionotropic preNMDAR boosting of release relies on RIM1αβ.
source: This boosting relies on RIM1αβ (Abrahamsson et al., 2017) and mTOR-mediated protein synthesis in L5 PC axons (Wong et al., 2024), yet is synapse-type-specific, so does not affect L5 PC→interneuron synapses (Buchanan et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ionotropic preNMDAR boosting of release relies on mTOR-mediated protein synthesis in L5 PC axons.
source: This boosting relies on RIM1αβ (Abrahamsson et al., 2017) and mTOR-mediated protein synthesis in L5 PC axons (Wong et al., 2024), yet is synapse-type-specific, so does not affect L5 PC→interneuron synapses (Buchanan et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Ionotropic preNMDAR boosting is synapse-type-specific and does not affect L5 PC→interneuron synapses.
source: This boosting relies on RIM1αβ (Abrahamsson et al., 2017) and mTOR-mediated protein synthesis in L5 PC axons (Wong et al., 2024), yet is synapse-type-specific, so does not affect L5 PC→interneuron synapses (Buchanan et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MK-801 blocks preNMDAR-mediated boosting of evoked L5 PC→PC release.
source: Consequently, MK-801 blocks preNMDAR-mediated boosting of evoked L5 PC→PC release (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Buchanan et al., 2012; Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Reduced Mg2+ does not elicit LTD but actually boosts neurotransmission at L5 PC→PC synapses.
source: In agreement, reduced Mg2+ does not elicit LTD but actually boosts neurotransmission (Abrahamsson et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PreNMDAR and CB1 receptor co-activation is required for L5 PC→PC tLTD.
source: As mentioned above, PreNMDAR and CB1 receptor co-activation is required for L5 PC→PC tLTD (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: L5 PC→PC tLTD does not depend on frequency.
source: Although L5 PC→PC tLTD does not depend on frequency (Sjöström et al., 2003), consistent with the non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling we provide evidence for here, chemical LTD (cLTD) induced by wash-in of cannabinoid CB1 receptor antagonists is, in fact, frequency dependent (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Chemical LTD induced by wash-in of cannabinoid CB1 receptor antagonists is frequency dependent.
source: Although L5 PC→PC tLTD does not depend on frequency (Sjöström et al., 2003), consistent with the non-ionotropic preNMDAR signaling we provide evidence for here, chemical LTD (cLTD) induced by wash-in of cannabinoid CB1 receptor antagonists is, in fact, frequency dependent (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: tLTD requires CB1 receptor signaling at low as well as high frequencies.
source: This apparent discrepancy is difficult to explain, because tLTD requires CB1 receptor signaling at low as well as high frequencies (Sjöström et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The frequency dependence of cLTD is consistent with its known sensitivity to MK-801.
source: Although the frequency dependence of cLTD is consistent with its known sensitivity to MK-801 (Sjöström et al., 2003), an apparent disagreement remains.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A potential explanation for the discrepancy is that CB1 receptor signaling in tLTD is phasic, whereas that in cLTD is tonic, and phasic/tonic CB1 signaling paths are known to differ mechanistically.
source: A potential explanation is that CB1 receptor signaling in tLTD is phasic, whereas that in cLTD is tonic, and phasic/tonic CB1 signaling paths are known to differ mechanistically (Castillo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as speculation supported by citation.

claim: The experiments were conducted in juvenile visual cortex.
source: Our experiments were conducted in juvenile visual cortex, so caution is warranted when extrapolating our findings to mature circuits, which may rely on different plasticity mechanisms (Banerjee et al., 2009; Corlew et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2014; Martínez-Gallego et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the study's scope.

claim: Mature circuits may rely on different plasticity mechanisms than juvenile circuits.
source: Our experiments were conducted in juvenile visual cortex, so caution is warranted when extrapolating our findings to mature circuits, which may rely on different plasticity mechanisms (Banerjee et al., 2009; Corlew et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2014; Martínez-Gallego et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: By engaging JNK2-mediated signaling independent of Ca2+ influx, preNMDARs contribute to STDP in a manner that has not been previously appreciated.
source: Our study provides a fresh perspective on non-ionotropic function for preNMDARs in tLTD at neocortical synapses. By engaging JNK2-mediated signaling independent of Ca2+ influx, preNMDARs contribute to STDP in a manner that has not been previously appreciated.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The findings highlight the diversity of synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
source: Our findings challenge the traditional view of NMDARs as coincidence detectors in Hebbian plasticity and highlight the diversity of synaptic plasticity mechanisms (Larsen and Sjöström, 2015; McFarlan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the study's findings.

claim: NMDARs are hotspots for major synaptic pathologies such as Alzheimer, schizophrenia, and epilepsy.
source: It is crucial to understand how NMDARs operate, as they are hotspots for major synaptic pathologies such as Alzheimer, schizophrenia, and epilepsy (Nugent et al., 2022; Paoletti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A central hypothesis in schizophrenia research is based on NMDAR hypofunction.
source: For instance, a central hypothesis in schizophrenia research is based on NMDAR hypofunction (Lisman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Sparse NMDAR deletion was achieved by removing the obligatory GluN1 subunit in a subset of L5 PCs by neonatal injection of AAV-eSYN-mCherry-iCre into V1 of Grin1fl/fl mice.
source: Sparse NMDAR deletion was achieved by removing the obligatory GluN1 subunit in a subset of L5 PCs by neonatal injection (Kim et al., 2014) of AAV-eSYN-mCherry-iCre into V1 of Grin1fl/fl mice (a.k.a. NR1flox) obtained from The Jackson Laboratory (#005246, see below), thus achieving sparse and conditional KO of the Grin1 gene in these mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: A Cre-loxP recombinase strategy was used to generate transgenic mice after two generations with the Rims1 gene homozygously conditionally deleted in excitatory cells.
source: A Cre-loxP recombinase strategy (Nagy, 2000) was used to generate transgenic mice after two generations with the Rims1 gene homozygously conditionally deleted in excitatory cells, as genome-wide Rims1 KO impairs survival (Mittelstaedt et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Genome-wide Rims1 KO impairs survival.
source: A Cre-loxP recombinase strategy (Nagy, 2000) was used to generate transgenic mice after two generations with the Rims1 gene homozygously conditionally deleted in excitatory cells, as genome-wide Rims1 KO impairs survival (Mittelstaedt et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The rate of connectivity in rodent primary visual cortex among L5 PCs is only 10–15%.
source: Since the rate of connectivity in rodent primary visual cortex among L5 PCs is only 10–15% (Sjöström et al., 2001; Song et al., 2005), quadruple whole-cell recording was employed to enable the simultaneous testing of 12 PC→PC connections (Abrahamsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Quadruple whole-cell recording was employed to enable the simultaneous testing of 12 PC→PC connections.
source: Since the rate of connectivity in rodent primary visual cortex among L5 PCs is only 10–15% (Sjöström et al., 2001; Song et al., 2005), quadruple whole-cell recording was employed to enable the simultaneous testing of 12 PC→PC connections (Abrahamsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: tLTD was induced by evoking postsynaptic firing 25ms before presynaptic firing, either at 20 Hz or at 1 Hz.
source: We induced tLTD by evoking postsynaptic firing 25ms before presynaptic firing, either at 20 Hz or at 1 Hz (Sjöström et al., 2001; Sjöström et al., 2003), which we refer to as HF and LF tLTD, respectively, throughout the present study.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: tLTP was induced by evoking presynaptic firing 10ms before postsynaptic cell firing at 50 Hz.
source: tLTP was induced by evoking presynaptic firing 10ms before postsynaptic cell firing at 50 Hz (Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.
